lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- Your Research in Ninety Seconds: The Pitch
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 14 -- Your Research in Ninety Seconds

paras: The idea of the elevator pitch is simple. Imagine that you enter an elevator with the director of a big research center. You have the time between two floors, about ninety seconds, to explain your work and make her interested. Most researchers fail this test for the same reason: they start with the method, and they never arrive at the result.

Good pitches have a clear shape. They open with a hook: a number, a question or a very short story that engages the listener. Then they highlight one result, not ten, and explain in one sentence why it matters. The best presenters tailor this middle part to the audience. For a specialist, they use the technical words. For everybody else, they simplify, and a phrase like "let me put it this way" gives them a second chance.

Finally, a good pitch ends with an invitation, not with a thank you. The speaker asks a question, offers a poster number or suggests a coffee. That is the moment when the conversation starts. If the listener wants more, you can always expand on the details later. What matters is that the takeaway is clear before the doors open.

listenings.text: Hello, I am Rahul Menon, and I work at a diabetes center in Chennai. In a nutshell, I study why small wounds on the feet of diabetic patients do not heal. Why does that matter? Because a wound that does not heal can lead to an amputation, and in India that happens to thousands of people every year. At the moment we are testing a very simple idea: a nurse checks the feet of every patient once a month. Last year, in our first clinic, the number of amputations went down by almost half. So my question for you is this: do you see the same problem in your country? If you do, I would love to compare our data.

Let me start with a number: one in five adults lives with pain every day. My name is Irina Volkova, and I am a physiotherapist in Kazan. Most people think that pain is only a signal from the body. Let me put it this way: pain is like an alarm, and sometimes the alarm is too sensitive. Our team works with patients who have back pain for more than a year. Since medicine alone did not help them, we added ten minutes of education to every session. We explained to them how pain works. As a result, after three months, more than half of them were moving better. Next year we are going to test the same program online. If you work with chronic pain, come and see my poster, number forty-two, this afternoon.
